results.seed: Links between Slaney's dimensions of perfectionism and the four humor styles of Martin et al. (2003)

harder.updated_question: Links between Slaney's dimensions of perfectionism and the four humor styles of Martin et al. (2003)
verification_criteria: Identifies and describes at least two of Slaney's dimensions of perfectionism (e.g., standards, discrepancy, order)
Identifies and describes all four humor styles from Martin et al. (2003): affiliative, self-enhancing, aggressive, and self-defeating
Reports empirical findings or theoretical connections linking specific perfectionism dimensions to specific humor styles

attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of how Slaney’s dimensions of perfectionism interface with Martin et al.’s (2003) four humor styles, drawing on psychometric definitions, cross-sectional associations, and mechanisms from personality and emotion-regulation literatures.

Overview and key definitions
- Martin et al.’s model conceptualizes humor use along two orthogonal dimensions: (i) target (self vs others), and (ii) benevolence (benign vs detrimental), yielding four styles: affiliative (others, benign), self-enhancing (self, benign), aggressive (others, detrimental), and self-defeating (self, detrimental). <cite id="9d70b877-4">Martin’s model is based on two underlying dimensions: 1) the use of humor directed to self versus others, and 2) the use of benign versus detrimental humor; the combination yields affiliative, self-enhancing, aggressive, and self-defeating humor with clear behavioral descriptions and validated structure</cite> <cite id="0b2dfdbb-3">Affiliative and self-enhancing are adaptive (relationship-building and reappraisal), whereas aggressive and self-defeating are maladaptive (insulting, self-humiliation), with the former two other- or self-oriented respectively</cite> <cite id="9d70b877-2">The HSQ operationalizes affiliative and self-enhancing as adaptive, and aggressive and self-defeating as maladaptive, with parallel 16-item subscales rated on a 7-point scale</cite>.
- Slaney’s perfectionism framework distinguishes three dimensions: self-oriented (unrealistic standards for the self), socially prescribed (belief that others demand perfection), and perceived burdensomeness (feeling overweight/overdone as a burden to others), typically assessed by the Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (MPS) and its short forms. <cite id="5fb98006-0">The MPS assesses self-oriented, other-oriented, and socially prescribed perfectionism with reliable subscales; items index beliefs about high standards and perceived external demands, with higher scores indicating greater perfectionism</cite> <cite id="5fb98006-1">An MPS implementation shows strong internal consistency for self-oriented (α≈.86–.87), socially prescribed (≈.87–.83), and other-oriented (≈.82–.81) subscales</cite> <cite id="5fb98006-2">Self-oriented perfectionism emphasizes personal standards (e.g., “I aim to be perfect”), socially prescribed emphasizes perceived external expectations (“The people around me expect me to succeed”), and other-oriented targets expectations for others</cite>. In many samples, perceived burdensomeness is closely entwined with socially prescribed perfectionism and self-critical scrutiny, creating interpersonal strain that can color social behavior, including humor.

Direct empirical links between perfectionism and humor styles
- Across studies, perfectionism correlates with maladaptive humor styles and inversely or variably with affiliative/self-enhancing styles, with trait factors explaining additional variance beyond Big Three personality. <cite id="9d70b877-0">Humor styles accounted for a significant percentage of incremental variance over personality traits in predicting rigid, self-critical, and narcissistic perfectionism dimensions</cite> <cite id="9d70b877-3">Aggressive humor contributed most strongly for rigid perfectionism (β≈.41), with affiliative inversely related and self-defeating positively related; overall, humor styles explained significant incremental variance in rigid, self-critical, and narcissistic perfectionism</cite>.
- Directional patterns by perfectionistic subtype tend to cluster: rigid/perfectionistic strivers and narcissistic variants show elevated aggressive humor; self-critical perfectionists show more self-defeating humor; affiliative humor is generally inversely related to perfectionism, while self-enhancing shows weaker or null associations. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Rigid perfectionism was most associated with aggressive humor (0.41), followed by affiliative (inverse) and self-defeating (positive); self-critical perfectionism showed the strongest relation to self-defeating humor followed by affiliative (inverse); narcissistic perfectionism was most related to aggressive humor (0.46), with affiliative inverse and self-defeating positive</cite> <cite id="9d70b877-1">Affiliative humor showed inverse relationships with all three perfectionism dimensions, whereas self-enhancing humor did not show any association</cite>.
- These patterns replicate across different populations and instruments, and they align with broader trait links: aggressive/self-defeating styles relate to lower agreeableness/conscientiousness and higher neuroticism and darker personality facets, whereas affiliative/self-enhancing relate to positive adjustment and social competence. <cite id="0b2dfdbb-2">Aggressive and self-defeating humor are positively correlated with neuroticism and with darker traits (psychopathy, Machiavellianism), while affiliative and self-enhancing are positively linked to extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and psychological adjustment</cite> <cite id="0b2dfdbb-3">Aggressive humor is associated with higher neuroticism, lower agreeableness, greater Machiavellianism and psychopathy, and lower social competence; affiliative and self-enhancing relate to optimism and life satisfaction</cite> <cite id="0b2dfdbb-4">Positive humor styles (affiliative, self-enhancing) correlate with positive personality and self-esteem, whereas negative styles (aggressive, self-defeating) relate to aggressive behavior and lower social support</cite>.

Mapping Slaney’s dimensions to Martin’s styles: conceptual and empirical bridges
- Socially prescribed perfectionism (external, interpersonal demand) → Aggressive and affiliative humor tensions:
  - Mechanism: fear of imperfection and perceived scrutiny fosters contemptuous or appeasing humor. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Perfectionists who feel worthless unless perfect tend to use aggressive humor characterized by disparaging or manipulating others, with affiliative humor inversely associated</cite>.
  - Evidence: socially prescribed perfectionism shows strong links to aggressive humor; affiliative humor is generally inversely related across perfectionism dimensions, consistent with discomfort tolerating others’ amusement or perceived threat to standards. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Aggressive humor had the greatest contribution to rigid and narcissistic perfectionism; affiliative humor was inversely related across all three perfectionism dimensions</cite>.
  - Nuance: affiliative humor may serve to preempt criticism or maintain relationships under perfectionistic climates, but in many samples its association with perfectionism is negative, suggesting it may also signal insincere self-presentation when “too” congenial. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Affiliative humor showed inverse relationships with all three perfectionism dimensions</cite> <cite id="0b2dfdbb-3">Affiliative humor aims to amuse without annoying, yet in perfectionistic contexts its inverse relation suggests it may not fit</cite>.
- Self-oriented perfectionism (internal standards, self-criticism) → Self-defeating and self-enhancing humor:
  - Mechanism: harsh self-evaluation and need for approval motivate either self-deprecating humor (to deflect judgment) or humor reappraisal (to cope). <cite id="5fb98006-0">Self-oriented perfectionism reflects unrealistic self-standards and hard self-evaluations</cite> <cite id="0b2dfdbb-3">Self-defeating humor is self-directed, intended to gain approval via self-humiliation, whereas self-enhancing reappraises stressors to cope</cite>.
  - Evidence: self-critical perfectionism shows the strongest relation to self-defeating humor and some positive relation to affiliative humor, with self-enhancing often weak or null; perceived burdensomeness/self-criticism co-occur with self-defeating tendencies. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Self-critical perfectionism showed the greatest contribution from self-defeating humor, followed by affiliative (inverse), while self-enhancing showed no association</cite> <cite id="9d70b877-1">Perfectionists with excessive self-criticism appear to use self-defeating humor and, to a lesser extent, affiliative humor</cite>.
  - Cross-trait pattern: self-oriented perfectionism co-varies with neuroticism and low agreeableness, aligning with higher aggressive/self-defeating styles relative to affiliative/self-enhancing. <cite id="0b2dfdbb-2">Aggressive and self-defeating styles correlate with neuroticism and lower agreeableness/conscientiousness</cite> <cite id="9d70b877-3">Rigid perfectionism’s strongest link is aggressive humor; self-critical shows self-defeating dominance</cite>.
- Other-oriented perfectionism (standards for others) and perceived burdensomeness (feeling overburdening relationships) → Affiliative and aggressive humor interplay:
  - Mechanism: high standards for others can drive either inclusive, relationship-maintaining humor or contempt/sarcasm toward “failures,” depending on benevolence. <cite id="0b2dfdbb-3">Aggressive humor targets superiority and diminishes others via sarcasm and disrespect; affiliative builds relationships and amuses without annoyance</cite>.
  - Evidence: other-oriented perfectionism is a distinct MPS dimension capturing demands on others; socially prescribed perfectionism (beliefs about external demands) shows robust ties to aggressive humor, with affiliative often inversely related, implying interpersonal control or appeasement dynamics rather than genuine affiliation. <cite id="5fb98006-2">Other-oriented perfectionism assesses unrealistic standards for others</cite> <cite id="5fb98006-0">Socially prescribed perfectionism reflects belief that others expect perfection</cite> <cite id="9d70b877-1">Aggressive humor contributes most for rigid (often linked to higher expectations of others) and narcissistic perfectionism; affiliative is inversely related</cite>.
  - Perceived burdensomeness (a Slaney concept often assessed indirectly via MPS components) can amplify aggressive tendencies (self- or other-focused) when individuals fear being a drain and use self-deprecating humor to reduce relational strain, or conversely, adopt rigidly “helpful” affiliative banter that is controlling rather than genuinely benign. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Perfectionists who feel worthwhile only when perfect use aggressive humor; those with self-critical burdensomeness lean toward self-defeating humor</cite> <cite id="0b2dfdbb-3">Self-defeating humor seeks approval via self-humiliation; affiliative aims at non-annoying amusement</cite>.
- Summary mapping across styles:
  - Affiliative humor: generally inversely associated with socially prescribed and self-oriented perfectionism (especially when humor feels inauthentic), though some positive links with other-oriented/adaptive self-presentation may appear. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Affiliative humor showed inverse relationships with all three perfectionism dimensions</cite> <cite id="0b2dfdbb-3">Affiliative humor fosters relationships without annoyance; maladaptive styles are linked to lower agreeableness and social competence</cite>.
  - Self-enhancing humor: weak or null association with perfectionism overall; protective when stressors are reframed, less aligned with self-critical cycles. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Self-enhancing humor showed no association with perfectionism dimensions in contrast to affiliative’s inverse pattern</cite>.
  - Aggressive humor: strongest positive link with rigid and narcissistic perfectionism; reflects superiority-seeking and devaluation consistent with high external/ideal standards and hostile scrutiny. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Aggressive humor’s contribution was largest for rigid perfectionism (0.41) and narcissistic perfectionism (0.46)</cite>.
  - Self-defeating humor: strongest link with self-critical perfectionism; serves approval-seeking via self-humiliation under harsh self-critique and perceived burdensomeness. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Self-critical perfectionism showed the greatest contribution from self-defeating humor</cite>.

Mechanisms and moderators: how and why the links emerge
- Trait dispositions: perfectionism co-varies with neuroticism and lower agreeableness/conscientiousness, aligning with higher aggressive/self-defeating styles and lower affiliative/self-enhancing; hostility and Machiavellian tendencies further link to aggressive humor. <cite id="0b2dfdbb-2">Aggressive and self-defeating humor correlate with neuroticism and with darker traits like psychopathy/Machiavellianism; affiliative/self-enhancing align with positive traits and adjustment</cite> <cite id="0b2dfdbb-3">Aggressive humor relates to higher neuroticism and lower agreeableness; self-defeating relates to lower social competence; affiliative/self-enhancing relate to optimism and life satisfaction</cite>.
- Self-worth contingencies: feeling worthy only through perfection fosters devaluing others (aggressive) or self-deprecation (self-defeating) to preserve fragile self-esteem; affiliative humor tends to feel inauthentic when it conflicts with self-criticism. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Perfectionists who feel worthwhile only when perfect use aggressive humor; self-critical perfectionists favor self-defeating and affiliative (inversely), with self-enhancing unrelated</cite>.
- Social comparison and approval motives: aggressive and self-defeating styles serve social comparison motives (superiority or acceptance), consistent with perfectionism’s emphasis on outperforming standards and avoiding rejection. <cite id="0b2dfdbb-3">Aggressive humor seeks superiority over others and diminishes their value; self-defeating humor gains approval via self-humiliation</cite> <cite id="0b2dfdbb-2">Aggressive/self-defeating styles relate to lower social competence and higher neuroticism, consistent with interpersonal strain</cite>.
- Personality and EI context: humor style–perfectionism links are incremental over broader traits and can be moderated by self-esteem and emotion-regulation strategies. <cite id="9d70b877-0">Humor styles explained incremental variance beyond Big Three traits in predicting perfectionism dimensions</cite> <cite id="0b2dfdbb-1">Self-defeating humor correlates negatively with self-esteem, while affiliative/self-enhancing show distinct validity patterns</cite>.

Practical implications and testable predictions
- Screening and assessment: measure Slaney’s dimensions with MPS (or SPS subscales) and HSQ; expect higher socially prescribed and self-oriented perfectionism to predict higher aggressive and self-defeating scores and lower affiliative scores, with self-enhancing hovering near zero in self-critical forms. <cite id="5fb98006-0">MPS subscales reliably capture socially prescribed and self-oriented perfectionism</cite> <cite id="9d70b877-1">Aggressive and self-defeating styles rise with rigid/self-critical perfectionism, while affiliative falls</cite> <cite id="9d70b877-2">HSQ provides validated subscales for affiliative/self-enhancing (adaptive) and aggressive/self-defeating (maladaptive)</cite>.
- Interventions: affiliative and self-enhancing humor training may reduce rigid/self-critical patterns by increasing benign humor use and reappraisal; targets could include challenging “only good when perfect” beliefs and modeling non-contemptuous banter. <cite id="9d70b877-0">Humor styles add incremental prediction beyond personality, suggesting leverage points for strengths-based intervention</cite> <cite id="9d70b877-1">Self-enhancing shows no association with self-critical perfectionism, hinting at potential for change</cite>.
- Moderators to probe: include neuroticism, agreeableness, self-esteem, and perceived social support/hostility; test mediation by emotion-regulation (rumination/self-blame) and approval-seeking motives. <cite id="0b2dfdbb-2">Aggressive/self-defeating humor links to neuroticism and lower agreeableness; affiliative/self-enhancing to adjustment</cite> <cite id="0b2dfdbb-4">Positive humor styles correlate with self-esteem and positive personality</cite> <cite id="0b2dfdbb-1">Self-defeating humor negatively correlates with self-esteem</cite>.

Limitations and future evidence
- Gaps: Few studies explicitly parameterize “perceived burdensomeness” separately from socially prescribed perfectionism when mapping to humor styles; most empirical links aggregate “rigid” and “self-critical” into socially prescribed/self-oriented categories. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Findings are reported for rigid, self-critical, and narcissistic perfectionism rather than perceived burdensomeness per se</cite>.
- Needed tests: Longitudinal and experimental work that (i) isolates perceived burdensomeness via experimental burden manipulation, (ii) fits structural models linking perfectionism → rumination/self-blame → humor choice, and (iii) tests whether affiliative/self-enhancing humor training causally shifts perfectionistic cognitions and behaviors. <cite id="9d70b877-0">Incremental predictive power suggests intervention potential but does not establish causality</cite>.

Summary link diagram
- Socially prescribed perfectionism (external demands, fear of failing others) → higher aggressive humor (superiority/contempt), often lower affiliative (genuine) → co-occur with low agreeableness and high neuroticism. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Aggressive humor most predictive for rigid/narcissistic perfectionism; affiliative inversely related</cite> <cite id="0b2dfdbb-2">Aggressive/self-defeating linked to neuroticism and darker traits; affiliative/self-enhancing to adjustment</cite>.
- Self-oriented/perceived-burden perfectionism (internal standards, self-criticism) → higher self-defeating humor (self-deprecation for approval) and weaker/positive affiliative; self-enhancing often unrelated or adaptive target for intervention. <cite id="9d70b877-1">Self-critical perfectionism shows strongest self-defeating link; affiliative negative; self-enhancing unrelated</cite>.
- Other-oriented perfectionism (standards for others) → may express aggressive humor toward “failures” and affiliative humor aimed at compliance, but overall patterns track with aggressive dominance when standards are punitive. <cite id="5fb98006-2">Other-oriented perfectionism reflects unrealistic expectations for others</cite> <cite id="9d70b877-1">Aggressive humor’s contribution rises with rigid perfectionism linked to higher expectations of others</cite>.
- Adaptive counterpoints: boosting affiliative and self-enhancing humor (relationship-building and reappraisal) is predicted to attenuate maladaptive perfectionistic cycles by shifting from devaluing/control to benign humor. <cite id="0b2dfdbb-3">Affiliative and self-enhancing humor are associated with positive interpersonal outcomes and psychological adjustment</cite> <cite id="9d70b877-0">Humor styles explain incremental variance beyond broad traits, supporting strengths-based intervention</cite>.

attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of research on superpixel- and segmentation-based methods that help visual generative models, covering image and video, mechanisms (conditioning, guidance, latent priors), empirical benefits, and open challenges.

1) Why structured superpixel/segmentation priors matter for generative models
Structured primitives like superpixels provide compact, semantically meaningful constraints that can improve controllability, conditioning efficiency, and semantic alignment in generative models, compared to pixel-level signals alone. <cite id="199c3c84-0">Diffusion-based image generation supports fine-grained control via guidance functions and conditioning signals such as segmentation masks, style, and object location, enabling alignment of generated content to explicit structural priors</cite>. <cite id="199c3c84-4">ControlNet formalizes this by learning to map auxiliary structure (edges, masks, depth, or features) to image outputs, leveraging pre-trained diffusion backbones to enhance quality and alignment for tasks like segmentation data augmentation</cite>. In the video domain, superpixel/supervoxel methods provide per-frame perceptual regions and temporal streaming extensions, enabling region-level edits and consistency planning across frames. <cite id="2bf7707f-2">Temporal superpixels compute superpixel segmentations on the first frame and extend them frame-by-frame via motion modeling (e.g., Gaussian Process with bilateral kernels), yielding streaming supervoxel segmentations that can be used as structured priors for downstream processing</cite>.

2) Superpixels and segmentation as conditioning/control for image generative models
Recent diffusion frameworks demonstrate that segmentation-like priors (masks, edges, depth, flow) can strongly constrain generation, often without retraining, via guidance and conditioning. <cite id="199c3c84-0">Guided diffusion integrates external supervision alongside original conditioning through a guidance function; classifier and classifier-free guidance steer outputs toward desired classes or text, and a broad set of universal constraints (segmentation masks, style, object location) have been applied within a unified framework</cite>. <cite id="199c3c84-1">ControlNet enables precise alignment between ground-truth segmentation masks and generated content, and when guided with active learning–style metrics during backward diffusion, the resulting synthetic samples improve segmentation model performance over non-guided synthetic data</cite>. <cite id="199c3c84-4">ControlNet’s incorporation of structural priors improves quality and alignment and is valuable for semantic segmentation augmentation, though it can struggle with complex multi-object scenes unless adapted (e.g., inpainting-style per-instance redrawing)</cite>. Beyond pixel/edge/flow, semantic segmentation itself has been formulated as conditional generation with latent priors: <cite id="544d51fd-0">Diffusion-based segmentation approaches leverage stable diffusion as a generative prior, with methods that unify generation and segmentation or directly condition diffusion on segmentation without text, showing that diffusion’s training stability can benefit segmentation as a conditional generation task</cite>. <cite id="544d51fd-2">Generative Semantic Segmentation (GSS) uses a VQ-VAE to project images and masks into a shared latent space and trains an encoder/decoder to map mask-latent distributions to image-latent encodings, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on public datasets while learning semantic structure in the discrete latent code</cite>. attempts.answer:
Summary
- Short answer: For standard diagnostic criteria, autism spectrum disorder requires symptoms to be present in early childhood, with DSM-5 specifying that onset is by approximately 3 years of age, while ICD-11 allows for retrospective recognition even if symptoms are not fully apparent until later due to demand–capacity mismatches; in practice, universal screening is recommended at 18 and 24 months to enable diagnosis before age 3 when benefits are greatest. <cite id="64cc6858-0">DSM-5 requires that symptoms start in early childhood and may not be fully manifest until later, with caution that they may only become evident during middle school, late adolescence, or young adulthood</cite> <cite id="0b1f29d8-0">ICD-11 moved to a more flexible onset criterion allowing later symptom emergence or retrospective recognition, while still classifying ASD as a developmental disorder because symptoms typically manifest within the first two years of life</cite> <cite id="7656985a-1">The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends universal screening at 18 and 24 months to support early diagnosis and access to intensive therapies before age 3</cite>.

DSM-5/DSM-5-TR criteria on onset age
- DSM-5 redefined ASD as a single diagnosis with persistent deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors, and maintains that these symptoms start in early childhood; importantly, it cautions that characteristic symptoms “may not be fully manifest until social demands exceed capacity,” which can occur during middle school, late adolescence, or young adulthood. This preserves the requirement that symptoms are present by age 3 in typical cases, even if they are only recognized later. <cite id="64cc6858-0">Symptoms start in early childhood, but may not be fully manifest until later, including during middle school, late adolescence, or young adulthood</cite>.
- Prior DSM-IV-TR had explicit subtypes (e.g., autistic disorder, Asperger’s) and required onset before 36 months for autistic disorder, but DSM-5 removed rigid age cutoffs to better capture high-functioning profiles while still considering ASD to manifest by toddlerhood (typically 12–24 months). Contemporary reviews emphasize that DSM-5’s change aimed at consistency across the spectrum, not erasing early-onset biology. <cite id="64cc6858-4">In DSM-IV-TR, autistic disorder should manifest before 36 months, but DSM-5 removed explicit age-of-onset specifications because of high-functioning cases; nonetheless ASD is regarded as manifesting by toddlerhood, typically between 12 and 24 months</cite>.

ICD-11 approach to onset and recognition
- ICD-11 consolidates prior pervasive developmental disorders into a single ASD diagnosis and requires that impairment begins during the developmental period, typically in early childhood. It explicitly acknowledges that symptoms may not become fully evident until later (e.g., adolescence or adulthood) when demands exceed limited capacities, enabling retrospective or “later” diagnoses when earlier signs were masked or missed. <cite id="0b1f29d8-1">ICD-11 requires onset in the developmental period, typically in early childhood, but recognizes that core symptoms may not become fully manifested until later, such as during early adolescence or adulthood due to demand–capacity mismatches</cite>.
- ICD-11 therefore allows for clinical recognition at any age if there is clear evidence that deficits originated in early development, while emphasizing that ASD is a developmental disorder with symptoms often detectable in the first two years of life. <cite id="0b1f29d8-0">ICD-11 implements a flexible developmental onset criterion allowing later emergence or retrospective recognition; symptoms typically manifest within the first two years of life even if not fully apparent at first</cite> <cite id="0b1f29d8-4">Autism is typically diagnosed early in childhood in ICD-11, with core impairments present from early development; many children show early developmental problems before diagnosis</cite>.

Clinical guidance (AAP) and real-world timing
- The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends ongoing developmental surveillance and universal ASD screening at 18 and 24 months to identify impairments early, enabling access to intensive behavioral interventions and special education before age 3. <cite id="7656985a-1">AAP recommends developmental surveillance and universal screening at 18 and 24 months, with comprehensive evaluation early to access intensive therapies before age 3</cite>.
- Despite screening, many children are formally diagnosed around age 5 in community data, with delays linked to subtler presentations, co-occurring conditions, and missed early red flags. <cite id="7656985a-3">Many children receive a formal diagnosis around age 5; diagnosis is delayed when symptoms are subtle, intellectual capacity is high, or coexisting psychiatric conditions overshadow autism features</cite> <cite id="7656985a-4">Mean age of diagnosis in high-resource settings commonly ranges from 50–60 months; severity, language delay, and socioeconomic factors are associated with earlier diagnosis</cite>.
- Programs emphasize that earlier referral and evaluation can reduce diagnostic delay; however, missed cases and prolonged delays persist. <cite id="7656985a-1">Even with early screening, there continues to be missed cases and significant time delays in formal neurodevelopmental evaluation and diagnosis before age 3</cite>.

Adults and “later” diagnoses: what counts
- In contemporary criteria, an adult can receive an ASD diagnosis if there is sufficient evidence that deficits originated in early development, even if they were not recognized until later due to demand–capacity mismatch, masking by skills, or comorbidities. ICD-11 explicitly permits retrospective recognition and “later” manifestation language, while DSM-5 underscores that “onset” is in early childhood even when symptoms become apparent later. <cite id="0b1f29d8-1">ICD-11 permits later manifestation and retrospective recognition when social demands exceed capacity</cite> <cite id="64cc6858-0">DSM-5 notes that symptoms may not be fully manifest until later despite onset in early childhood</cite>.
- Nonetheless, reviews and clinical cohorts show that ASD is typically diagnosable from toddlerhood onward, with many diagnoses occurring around preschool or later; persistent language delay, regression, or behavioral red flags in the first two years heighten concern and support earlier identification. <cite id="7656985a-3">Autism can be identified from early infancy through school age, but formal diagnoses often occur later due to subtler presentations</cite> <cite id="0b1f29d8-0">Symptoms often manifest within the first two years, enabling ASD to be recognized at any age with retrospective insight</cite>.
- Some adults retrospectively interpret childhood behaviors (e.g., uneven social development, fixated interests) as consistent with ASD, but validity depends on documented early developmental concerns and developmental course; high IQ or “mild” social difficulties can mask ASD and lead to misattribution to ADHD, anxiety, or learning disabilities. <cite id="7656985a-3">Coexisting psychiatric conditions and subtle presentations can delay recognition, making older children and adults harder to diagnose and increasing the risk of overshadowing by other problems</cite>.

Practical implications
- Families and clinicians: monitor for red flags by 12–18 months and seek evaluation by 24 months; if concerns arise later, pursue comprehensive ASD assessment and developmental history to uncover earlier subtle signs; persistent social-communication deficits and restricted/repetitive behaviors that impair functioning, even without clear early delay, warrant evaluation under current criteria. <cite id="7656985a-1">AAP universal screening at 18 and 24 months supports early detection and access to intensive interventions before age 3</cite> <cite id="64cc6858-0">DSM-5 criteria require onset in early childhood, with possible later full manifestation</cite> <cite id="0b1f29d8-1">ICD-11 allows later recognition if impairment originated in early development</cite>.
- Documentation and longitudinal records: early EI evaluations, pediatric visits, and school observations can reveal developmental trajectories that substantiate an early onset despite late recognition. <cite id="7656985a-1">Missed cases and delays persist despite screening, underscoring the need for strong networks across pediatric care, early intervention, and diagnostics</cite>.

Bottom line
- Diagnoses based on DSM-5/DSM-5-TR require that autism symptoms emerge in early childhood, typically by age 3, even if they are not fully apparent until later; ICD-11 permits retrospective diagnosis when symptoms first arose in early development and later became manifest due to increased social demands or masking. Clinical guidelines emphasize screening by 18–24 months to enable early diagnosis and intervention, with many children still being diagnosed around age 5 in practice due to subtlety of symptoms, co-occurring problems, or missed early signs. <cite id="64cc6858-0">DSM-5 requires start in early childhood and acknowledges later full manifestation</cite> <cite id="0b1f29d8-1">ICD-11 requires developmental onset but allows later manifestation and retrospective recognition</cite> <cite id="7656985a-1">AAP recommends universal screening at 18 and 24 months to support early diagnosis</cite> <cite id="7656985a-3">Many formal diagnoses occur around age 5 when symptoms are subtle or masked</cite>.

attempts.answer:
Below is an evidence-backed synthesis of how inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) pathology points to nanobot intervention opportunities, how nanobots can serve as delivery systems with advantages over traditional routes, and which immune-modulation strategies are being explored specifically to reduce inflammation.

1) Key pathological features of IBD that point to nanobot targets
- IBD pathogenesis centers on chronic mucosal inflammation driven by dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity, with key cytokine nodes including TNF-α, IL‑1 family, and IL‑6/TGF‑β/IL‑23–dependent Th17 axis; epithelial barrier dysfunction and microbiome dysbiosis further fuel immune activation and disease susceptibility to relapse and nonresponse to therapy <cite id="01cbdfcf-0">Inflammatory bowel disease pathogenesis highlights mucosal barrier dysfunction, dysregulated immune responses, genetic predisposition, and the fecal microbiota; IL‑12 and IL‑23 drive Th1/Th17 responses</cite> <cite id="01cbdfcf-3">Cells of innate and adaptive immunity drive cytokine pathways in IBD mucosa; principal cytokines include TNF‑α, IL‑8 (innate) and Th1/Th2/Th17 cytokines with anti‑inflammatory IL‑10 and Tregs</cite> <cite id="01cbdfcf-4">Activation of Th1/Th17 and macrophages/dendritic cells increases proinflammatory cytokines; IL‑12 and IL‑23 are crucial in Crohn’s; NF‑κB mediates production of IL‑12, IL‑23, TNF‑α, IL‑6, IL‑8, IL‑1β</cite>.
- Inflammasome activation, particularly NLRP3-driven maturation of IL‑1β, promotes Th17 responses and worsens colitis; reduced Nlrp3 activity lowers IL‑1β and Th17 immunity and ameliorates disease in murine models, positioning NLRP3/IL‑1β as mechanistic targets for intervention <cite id="01cbdfcf-1">UC shows elevated Th1/Th2/Th17 markers and increased NLRP3/Caspase‑1/IL‑1β correlating with severity; the NLRP3/T‑bet/GATA3 axis is a candidate for multi‑targeted therapy</cite> <cite id="01cbdfcf-2">IL‑1β, produced by NLRP3‑activated myeloid cells, induces Th17 polarization and reduces tolerogenic CD103+ DC; Nlrp3 deficiency lowers IL‑1β, reduces Th17 immunity, and lessens colitis in T cell transfer colitis</cite>.
- Clinical refractory disease—primary/secondary nonresponse to TNF‑α inhibitors—highlights the need for alternative, site‑specific immune modulation and mucosal delivery strategies that can reach targets not modulated by systemic biologics <cite id="01cbdfcf-0">Around 10–20% are primary non‑responders and 23–46% secondary non‑responders to TNF‑α inhibitors; mucosal healing and immune/microbiome targets are emphasized</cite>.

2) How nanobots can be employed as delivery systems in IBD, and their advantages over traditional methods
- Microrobots/nanomotors can reach the inflamed colon after oral administration, traverse mucosal and tissue barriers, and provide precise, on‑demand drug release in response to external controls or local inflammatory cues (pH, enzymes, oxygen, magnetic fields), improving drug bioavailability at lesion sites and reducing systemic exposure <cite id="46dd8ffc-0">Micro/nanomotors enter via oral administration, traverse mucosal/tissue barriers to lesion sites, and regulate release via external or biological‑milieu triggers, reducing side effects and increasing efficacy</cite> <cite id="4199c8ec-0">Nanoparticles’ small size and surface properties facilitate tissue penetration and targeted/controlled release; orally administered particles show enhanced adherence in inflamed colonic tissue versus healthy tissue in preclinical models</cite> <cite id="4199c8ec-4">Colon’s neutral pH, prolonged transit, low proteases, and sensitivity to enhancers favor targeted oral delivery; oral route is preferred over rectal due to simplicity but faces GIT degradation and mucus penetration challenges</cite>.
- Advantages over conventional oral/rectal and systemic strategies include protection from gastric and enzymatic degradation, enhanced mucus/biofilm penetration, active targeting to sites of inflammation, and controlled or triggered release that can concentrate drug at the colon while limiting healthy‑tissue exposure; these features address core IBD delivery barriers that reduce drug availability at the mucosa <cite id="4199c8ec-1">Nanoparticle‑based DDS can improve colon targeting and efficacy while reducing systemic toxicity; oral delivery to colon is desirable but challenged by mucus/epithelium barriers</cite> <cite id="4199c8ec-2">Smart, responsive nanocarriers (pH/ROS/enzyme/thermo) enable selective release, avoiding systemic absorption and minimizing delivery to healthy tissue; multi‑responsive systems enhance targeting and uptake</cite> <cite id="4199c8ec-3">Oral nanomedicines improve uptake in diseased colon segments; size, mucoadhesive charge, PEGylation, pH/redox‑responsive designs augment colon targeting; specialized epithelial M cells and gaps in villous tips facilitate translocation</cite> <cite id="46dd8ffc-3">Catalase‑powered nanobots use H2O2 for propulsion and mucin disruption; combined mucin disruption and self‑propulsion enable rapid (15 min) mucus penetration relevant to fast mucus turnover</cite>.
- Comparative perspective: traditional rectal routes can suffer from uneven drug distribution to the colon; oral nanosystems aim to overcome variable colon coverage and GIT degradation with colon‑specific triggers and enhancer sensitivity, while microrobots add motility and local actuation to further skew drug exposure to inflamed tissue <cite id="4199c8ec-4">Rectal forms often have limited effectiveness due to variable distribution; oral route is preferred but requires protection from degradation and improved mucus permeation</cite> <cite id="46dd8ffc-0">MNMs traverse mucosal layers and tissue barriers and regulate release by external or local cues to enhance bioavailability and therapeutic effect</cite>.
- Demonstrated preclinical gains: enzyme‑driven nanomotors (e.g., twin‑bioengine yeast robots) that exploit intestinal glucose and chemokine gradients reached intestinal walls within minutes with ~1000‑fold drug accumulation at lesions, reducing inflammation and improving pathology in mouse ulcerative colitis and gastric cancer models, highlighting the potential of chemotactic, targeted delivery to inflamed tissue <cite id="46dd8ffc-1">TBY‑robots penetrate mucus via dual enzyme‑driven mechanism, chemotact toward glucose gradients at 16.74 μm/s; enzyme‑enhanced delivery increased lesion accumulation ~1000‑fold and reduced inflammation, improving disease pathology in mouse UC/GC models</cite>.
- Additional microrobot modalities: magnetic and photo‑controlled devices can be parked or activated in vivo; payloads can be coated for timed diffusion, and platforms can be expanded to sensors and microsurgical biopsy functions, positioning them for future localized anti‑inflammatory regimens guided by imaging and real‑time control <cite id="46dd8ffc-2">Tumbling magnetic microrobots show in vivo locomotion, imaging visibility, and passive payload diffusion; future drugs can be coated for timed release at target sites; platforms could measure microbiota, carry microsensors, or perform minimally invasive biopsies</cite>.

3) Immune‑modulation strategies under exploration with nanobots for IBD
- Delivering biologics directly to inflamed mucosa: nanocarriers and nanomotors can encapsulate proteins/cytokines (e.g., anti‑TNF, IL‑10) and protect them from GIT degradation while enhancing local concentration; oral nanomedicine has shown preferential accumulation in inflamed colonic segments in preclinical models, addressing systemic exposure and first‑pass losses <cite id="4199c8ec-0">Orally administered nanoparticles show enhanced adherence in inflamed colonic tissues compared to healthy tissues, enabling targeted and controlled release</cite> <cite id="4199c8ec-1">Oral colon‑targeted nanocarriers improve efficacy and reduce systemic toxicity for UC</cite> <cite id="46dd8ffc-2">Microrobot payload coatings allow timed release at the desired in vivo location, with future loading of actual drugs</cite>.

attempts.answer:
Overview and clinical motivation
Asthma pathophysiology involves chronic airway inflammation and structural remodeling, with airway smooth muscle cells (ASMCs) contributing to hyperresponsiveness, airflow obstruction, and remodeling through proliferation, migration, hypertrophy, and secretion of mediators that perpetuate inflammation and matrix remodeling.<cite id="dfc3ed18-0">Determining the mechanisms responsible for ASMC abnormalities—such as hyperplasia and hypertrophy—is vital, and noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs and long noncoding RNAs, have been linked to ASMC dysregulation and proposed as diagnostic/treatment targets</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">Muscle-enriched microRNAs (miR-1, miR-133 family) can function in asthma by regulating bronchial smooth muscle cells and pathways such as Jak/STAT, with miR-133a downregulation correlating with increased RhoA and contractility associated with airway hyperresponsiveness</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">Systemic inflammatory cell lineages (e.g., T cells, epithelial cells, eosinophils, mast cells, macrophages, neutrophils) are also targets of miRNAs in asthma, supporting a multi-cellular regulatory network</cite>.

Current status of microRNA research in airway smooth muscle and asthma
Mechanistic roles in contractile regulation and phenotype. Multiple miRNAs modulate ASMC contractility, proliferation, and inflammatory phenotype. <cite id="73d84cbc-1">MiR-133a is decreased in lung sections of asthmatic mice; overexpression of miR-133a reduces airway remodeling, and RyR2—a childhood allergic asthma risk gene—is a target of miR-133a</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">Downregulation of miR-133a correlates with increased RhoA and elevated bronchial smooth muscle contractility associated with airway hyperresponsiveness</cite>.<cite id="73d84cbc-1">In ASMCs, MALAT1 knockdown decreases RyR2 expression and augments miR-133a levels, connecting an lncRNA–miRNA–target axis to calcium handling and contractile phenotype</cite>.

Proliferation, migration, and steroid responsiveness. <cite id="ae83b5d5-1">miR-221 downregulates p21WAF1 and p27KIP1, thereby relieving their growth-inhibitory function and favoring ASMC proliferation; this microRNA pathway was previously reported to underlie the aberrant ASMC phenotype in asthma</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">miR-26a promotes ASMC hypertrophy by suppressing the anti-hypertrophic kinase GSK-3β</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">miR-221 also increases IL-6 production in ASMCs, linking microRNA control to inflammatory mediator output</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">miR-146b-5p is highly expressed in ASMCs from asthmatics upon stimulation, indicating an inducible pro-remodeling state</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-4">Across mouse models of allergic asthma, functional loss- and gain-of-function studies implicate miR-21, miR-126, miR-145, miR-106a, miR-1, let-7, and miR-221 in disease processes via effects on cytokines and transcription factors</cite>.

Therapeutic modulation and translational signals. <cite id="ae83b5d5-1">In a mouse model of allergic airway disease, elevated miR-21 activates PI3K/AKT and inhibits HDAC2, contributing to steroid insensitivity; a miR-21 inhibitor reduces proliferation and migration of human ASMCs via PTEN/PI3K, linking miRNA function to steroid responsiveness</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-4">In combined allergic rhinitis and asthma models, lowering miR-21-5p reduces airway hyperresponsiveness and inflammation, supporting a causal role</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">Circulating muscle miRs correlate with disease activity and may serve as diagnostic biomarkers and systemic therapeutic targets, though autocrine and paracrine effects across airway cell types complicate interpretation</cite>.

Current status of long noncoding RNA research in airway smooth muscle and asthma
Immune–structural axis and NEAT1–miR-128. <cite id="ae83b5d5-2">In childhood asthma, lncRNA-NEAT1 is significantly upregulated in sputum while miR-128 is downregulated; NEAT1 negatively correlates with miR-128 and acts as an miRNA sponge, enhancing PDGF-BB–induced inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8), mesenchymal markers (α-SMA, calponin), matrix remodeling enzymes (MMP-2/9), and ASMC proliferation/migration in vitro</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-2">Dual-luciferase assays confirm direct targeting of miR-128 by NEAT1, establishing a ceRNA mechanism that drives phenotypic transformation of ASMCs</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">NEAT1 levels correlate with asthma severity, positioning it as a biomarker candidate</cite>.

PVT1 and corticosteroid sensitivity. <cite id="dfc3ed18-3">Using transcriptomics and functional targeting in human ASMCs from nonsevere (corticosteroid-sensitive) and severe (corticosteroid-insensitive) asthma, PVT1 is decreased in the sensitive group but increased in the resistant group; modulating PVT1 alters downstream gene programs, implicating a lncRNA mechanism in corticosteroid response of ASMCs</cite>.<cite id="dfc3ed18-3">This work extends earlier findings that miR-221 (which targets p21/p27) negatively regulates ASMC phenotypes, connecting miRNA control points to lncRNA-driven remodeling and steroid responsiveness</cite>.

MALAT1 and miR-133a/miR-216a axes. <cite id="73d84cbc-1">MALAT1 is increased in tracheal tissues of asthma models and in serum of asthmatic patients; MALAT1 knockdown in bronchial/smooth muscle cells decreases RyR2 and raises miR-133a, with miR-133a targeting RyR2, thereby repressing apoptosis and reducing IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β release via the miR-133a–RyR2 axis</cite>.<cite id="73d84cbc-2">Clinical serum profiling shows MALAT1 upregulation and miR-216a downregulation in asthma; inhibiting MALAT1 elevates miR-216a to promote apoptosis and suppress proliferation and migration in ASMCs</cite>.<cite id="73d84cbc-3">Mechanistically, MALAT1 sponges miR-216a to drive pro-remodeling ASMC phenotypes; targeting MALAT1 or boosting miR-216a is proposed as a therapeutic direction for airway remodeling</cite>.<cite id="73d84cbc-1">Consistent with this, miR-133a is reduced in asthmatic murine lung and its overexpression mitigates airway remodeling, aligning lncRNA–miRNA–protein logic with disease-modifying effects</cite>.

Additional lncRNA regulators of ASMC behavior. <cite id="73d84cbc-4">LNC_00882 is upregulated in ASMCs after PDGF stimulation and in neonatal asthmatic rat models; it sponges miR-3619-5p to relieve repression of β-catenin, thereby enhancing Wnt/β-catenin signaling and ASMC proliferation</cite>.<cite id="73d84cbc-4">MALAT1 is elevated in ASMCs after PDGF exposure and in neonatal asthmatic rat models, reinforcing its role in PDGF-driven remodeling pathways</cite>.

Cross-tissue ncRNA signals and systems-level regulation
Immune and epithelial contexts converge with ASM remodeling. <cite id="ae83b5d5-1">Muscle miRNAs coordinate with immune cell programs: miR-133b and miR-206 are expressed during Th17 differentiation with IL-17, linking muscle miRNAs to T cell subsets implicated in asthma</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">Cytokine mRNAs are targets of miRNAs in mast cells, eosinophils, macrophages, neutrophils, and airway epithelial cells, supporting a multi-cell ceRNA network that feeds into ASMC phenotypes</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">A pediatric allergic asthma miRNA signature implicates miR-370-3p targeting PKG and MLCP in the cGMP–PKG pathway, providing mechanistic insight into bronchodilator/anti-inflammatory signaling perturbation</cite>.<cite id="dfc3ed18-4">Broadly, ncRNAs (lncRNAs, miRNAs, circRNAs) act as competing endogenous RNA hubs in asthma, with ceRNA models explaining indirect miRNA repression by lncRNAs/circRNAs</cite>.

Clinical evidence and biomarker potential
Human and translational correlates are emerging. <cite id="ae83b5d5-1">Peripheral blood miR-1 levels correlate inversely with Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-8, TNF-α) and positively with IFN-γ in acute asthma, suggesting systemic miRNA control over inflammatory circuits relevant to ASM remodeling</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-2">Sputum NEAT1 upregulation and miR-128 downregulation in childhood asthma, together with functional rescue of inflammatory/phenotypic markers by NEAT1 knockdown, support biomarker and therapeutic hypotheses</cite>.<cite id="73d84cbc-2">MALAT1–miR-216a inverse expression in serum of asthmatics and rescue of ASMC apoptosis/proliferation by MALAT1 inhibition suggest combined biomarker–therapeutic utility</cite>.<cite id="dfc3ed18-3">Differential PVT1 expression linked to corticosteroid sensitivity in ASMCs suggests a route to stratify biologic therapy response via lncRNA readouts</cite>.

What is still missing and future directions
Evidence gaps. <cite id="ae83b5d5-1">Despite multiple mechanistic studies and correlations, few studies have profiled miRNAs directly in asthmatic human ASM tissue itself; most miRNA functional evidence in ASMCs comes from in vitro or murine models</cite>.<cite id="73d84cbc-1">For MALAT1, miR-133a, and miR-216a, strong in vivo links are shown in animal models or systemic compartments, but causal ASM-in situ interventions in humans remain limited</cite>.<cite id="dfc3ed18-3">Steroid responsiveness in ASMCs is tied to lncRNA PVT1, but translational validation in diverse asthma phenotypes (crackles, severe eosinophilic vs. nonresponder) is needed</cite>.

Therapeutic translation. <cite id="ae83b5d5-4">miRNA-based therapeutics have advanced in mouse allergic asthma via intratracheal/intranasal antagomiRs targeting miR-21, miR-126, miR-145, miR-106a, miR-1, let-7, and miR-221 with measurable effects on cytokines/transcription factors and airway inflammation</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">miR-21 inhibition reduces ASMC proliferation/migration via PTEN/PI3K and improves steroid insensitivity in preclinical models, motivating antisense or sponge-based lncRNA strategies that normalize miRNA–target axes</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-2">lncRNA sponges (e.g., NEAT1) and inhibitors (e.g., MALAT1) alter cytokine, contractility, and ECM profiles in ASMCs, supporting RNA-targeted ASMC therapy</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">However, circulating miRNA biomarkers face challenges of stability, cell-of-origin specificity, and systemic off-target effects; localized ASM delivery or synthetic RNA nanocarriers may be required</cite>.

Summary
- MicroRNAs and lncRNAs form a mechanistic and systems-level control layer over ASMC contractility, proliferation, inflammation, and steroid responsiveness in asthma, with convergent evidence from human clinical samples, ASMC models, and animal disease systems.<cite id="dfc3ed18-0">Noncoding RNAs have been associated with ASMC abnormalities and proposed for diagnostic and therapeutic strategies</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">Muscle miRNAs such as miR-1/133a/b regulate RhoA/contractility and inflammatory signaling in ASMCs; miR-221 controls p21/p27 and IL-6; miR-146b-5p is induced in stimulated ASMCs</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-2">lncRNA NEAT1 sponges miR-128 to amplify inflammatory and phenotypic transformation programs in ASMCs</cite>.<cite id="dfc3ed18-3">lncRNA PVT1 shows inverse expression with corticosteroid sensitivity in ASMCs and modulates downstream gene networks</cite>.<cite id="73d84cbc-1">lncRNA MALAT1 regulates miR-133a/RyR2 and miR-216a axes, affecting apoptosis, inflammation, and ASMC growth; clinical serum correlates support translational relevance</cite>.<cite id="73d84cbc-4">Additional lncRNAs such as LNC_00882/MALAT1 elevate Wnt/β-catenin signaling and ASMC proliferation in asthma-relevant models</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">System-level miRNA/lncRNA networks in immune and epithelial cells intersect with ASMC remodeling, and pediatric miRNA signatures implicate cGMP–PKG pathway perturbation</cite>.
- Therapeutically, multiple RNA targets are actionable: restoring downregulated miRNAs (e.g., miR-133a, miR-216a), inhibiting pro-disease miRNAs (e.g., miR-21, miR-221), or modulating lncRNAs (e.g., NEAT1, PVT1, MALAT1) to reverse ASMC hyperplasia/hypertrophy and inflammation; early data in animals and cell models are encouraging, but human in situ validation and localized delivery strategies are key next steps.<cite id="ae83b5d5-4">miRNA antagomiRs targeting multiple nodes reduce allergic airway disease features in mice</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">miR-21 inhibition reduces ASMC growth and improves steroid insensitivity</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-2">lncRNA sponges and knockdowns normalize inflammatory/phenotypic markers in ASMCs</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">Clinical correlations and biomarker potential exist, but translational challenges remain</cite>.
- Outstanding needs include large-cohort profiling of ncRNAs directly in human ASM tissue across asthma subphenotypes, causal in vivo ASM-targeted RNA therapeutics (with localized delivery), and integration of ceRNA/network models with single-cell atlases to map cell–cell RNA crosstalk driving remodeling.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">Few studies have examined miRNA expression in asthmatic human ASM tissue</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">Autocrine/paracrine effects and multi-cell targets complicate interpretation and design</cite>.<cite id="73d84cbc-3">Downstream targets of miR-216a in ASMCs and relationships to diagnosis/poor prognosis warrant future study</cite>.

Practical takeaways for asthma ASM-focused research
- Prioritize functional studies in primary human ASMCs from steroid-responsive vs.–resistant cohorts to map lncRNA/miRNA signatures that predict remodeling trajectory and therapy response (e.g., PVT1, NEAT1, MALAT1).<cite id="dfc3ed18-3">PVT1 differential expression associates with corticosteroid sensitivity in ASMCs</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-2">NEAT1/miR-128 dysregulation correlates with disease activity and inflammatory/phenotypic transformation</cite>.<cite id="73d84cbc-2">MALAT1/miR-216a serum signatures track ASMC growth programs</cite>.
- Develop localized RNA therapeutics (antisense/miRNA mimics, lncRNA sponges/inhibitors) tested first in ex vivo ASMCs and then in precision murine models (ovalbumin, HDM, IL-13) to reverse hyperplasia/hypertrophy and inflammation with steroid-sensitizing effects.<cite id="ae83b5d5-4">Intranasal/intratracheal antagomiRs have validated targets and phenotypes across allergic asthma models</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">miR-21 inhibitors reduce ASMC proliferation/migration and restore steroid responsiveness via PTEN/PI3K/HDAC2</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-2">lncRNA NEAT1/MALAT1 targeting normalizes cytokines, contractility markers, and migration</cite>.
- Integrate multi-omics and imaging of ASM to connect ncRNA perturbations to RhoA/contractility, Ca2+ signaling (RyR2), Wnt/β-catenin, and cGMP–PKG pathways, aligning with known targets for bronchodilators and anti-inflammatories.<cite id="73d84cbc-1">miR-133a targets RyR2 and is reduced in asthmatic lung, with overexpression reducing remodeling</cite>.<cite id="73d84cbc-2">MALAT1 sponges miR-216a to promote ASMC proliferation and migration</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">miR-370-3p targets PKG/MLCP in allergic asthma, intersecting with cGMP–PKG signaling</cite>.

In sum, ncRNA research has established clear mechanistic links between ASMC biology and asthma phenotypes, identified candidate biomarkers and therapeutic targets, and demonstrated proof-of-principle efficacy in models; the next phase will refine patient selection, deliver RNA-based interventions directly to ASM, and validate these axes in human tissue to realize clinical impact.<cite id="dfc3ed18-0">ncRNAs are poised to inform diagnostics and therapies via mechanistic maps of ASMC pathology</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-1">Muscle miRNAs, immune cell miRNAs, and lncRNA sponges modulate ASM remodeling and inflammation</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-2">lncRNA NEAT1 drives inflammatory/phenotypic transformation via miR-128 sequestration in ASMCs</cite>.<cite id="dfc3ed18-3">lncRNA PVT1 differentially regulates corticosteroid-sensitive versus -resistant ASMCs</cite>.<cite id="73d84cbc-1">lncRNA MALAT1–miR-133a/RyR2 and miR-216a axes connect systemic signatures to ASMC growth, apoptosis, and inflammation</cite>.<cite id="ae83b5d5-4">Preclinical RNA therapeutics provide a translational pipeline to test and refine these targets in asthma</cite>.

Below are Rickettsial effector proteins that target host organelles, grouped by organelle and accompanied by mechanistic evidence and representative examples.

Autophagosome/lysosome pathway
- Secreted effectors that modulate autophagosome formation and maturation: Pathogenic Rickettsia (e.g., R. typhi, R. rickettsii) induce autophagy yet evade lysosomal degradation via secreted effectors, including the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase Risk1 and phospholipases Pat1/Pat2, which alter membrane phosphoinositides critical for autophagosome biogenesis and trafficking, leading to LC3-positive but non-degradative compartments that shelter bacteria <cite id="2b287fb9-0">Pathogenic Rickettsia induce autophagy and then evade autolysosomal destruction via secreted effectors including phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase Risk1 and phospholipases Pat1 and Pat2, consistent with differential LC3B colocalization phenotypes in knockout macrophages</cite> <cite id="beef7575-3">R. typhi and R. rickettsii colocalize with LC3B in ATG5-deficient macrophages but not in control cells, whereas R. montanensis colocalizes with Lamp2 in ATG5-deficient cells, indicating distinct maturation states of autophagosome–lysosome pathways during infection</cite>. 
- Outer membrane proteins that promote autophagy evasion: In R. parkeri, the outer membrane protein B (rOmpB) blocks ubiquitylation of surface OmpA and suppresses autophagic recognition, enabling formation of a capsule-like structure that prevents autophagy and supports colonization; this directly links membrane-associated virulence factors to autophagosome pathway interference <cite id="2b287fb9-2">rOmpB blocks ubiquitylation of OmpA and autophagy recognition, is required for a capsule-like structure that blocks autophagy in macrophages, and promotes colonization in mice</cite>. 
- Generalized hijacking of autophagy by effectors: Reviews and comparative studies document that Rickettsia secrete effectors that modulate endoplasmic reticulum structures and hijack the autophagic defense pathway to establish replication niches, consistent with organelle-level subversion rather than simple replication within phagolysosomes <cite id="beef7575-2">Pathogenic Rickettsia secret effectors to modulate ER structures and to hijack autophagy and inflammasome pathways, enabling escape from phagosomes and establishment of intracytosolic replication niches</cite>.

Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
- Autotransporter effectors that remodel ER structure: The Rickettsia-secreted autotransporter RARP-2 (OmpA homolog) and related Sca/OmpA-family effectors are proposed to interact with and alter ER structure and membrane trafficking; ER remodeling contributes to pathogen survival and suppression of ER-stress apoptotic signaling early during infection <cite id="c5d8acbe-0">The RARP-2 effector, secreted via type IV secretion, has been proposed to interact with and alter host cell ER structure; early infection induces ER stress and cytochrome c release while Rickettsiae expand via ER-linked survival mechanisms</cite>. 
- Phosphoinositide effectors at ER and plasma membrane: R. typhi Risk1 is a dual-specificity PI3K that localizes to PI metabolism at ER and plasma membrane, promoting intracellular survival by coordinating membrane dynamics and trafficking during invasion; the Rickettsia vir homolog T4SS translocates RalF (Sec7-domain) to target phosphoinositide metabolism at the ER, reinforcing the ER’s role as a key effector-target organelle <cite id="beef7575-4">Rickettsia vir homolog T4SS translocates RalF, a Sec7-domain protein that targets phosphoinositide metabolism during invasion</cite> <cite id="beef7575-4">Risk1, a dual specificity phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase effector, promotes R. typhi intracellular survival by modulating PI metabolism, implicating ER and plasma membrane as targets</cite>. 
- Sca/OmpA repertoire and ER targeting: The sca gene family (sca0–sca5 encoding OmpA/OmpB-like autotransporters and intracellular domains) is expressed during adhesion/entry and is widely conserved across Rickettsia; comparative genomics reveals extensive diversification of sca genes, consistent with species-specific strategies for ER and membrane-trafficking subversion during uptake and early cytosolic survival <cite id="2b287fb9-3">sca genes encode active autotransporters (OmpA/OmpB and intracellular passenger domains) mediating adhesion and entry via host receptors such as Ku70 and integrins</cite> <cite id="c5d8acbe-4">sca genes (including sca1, sca4, sca5/ompB) are variably distributed across Rickettsia genomes with sca4 encoding a 120-kDa intracellular protein lacking the autotransporter domain, reflecting diversification of effector architectures</cite>. 
- Orientia homologs of Rickettsia OmpA: Orientia tsutsugamushi encodes OmpA homologs (OmpA, OmpD) with long cytosolic passenger domains analogous to sca effectors, and comparative studies show O. tsutsugamushi and Rickettsia share T4SS effectors (RalF, RARP-2) that modulate ER structures and phosphoinositide metabolism, supporting ER as a common organelle target across Rickettsiales <cite id="2b287fb9-0">R. typhi uses RalF and RARP-2 to modulate ER structures and PI metabolism during invasion, phenotypes echoed by O. tsutsugamushi’s OmpA/OmpD homologs and T4SS effectors</cite>. 

Mitochondria
- Membrane integrity and cytochrome c/apoptosis control: Early infection with Rickettsia induces cytochrome c release and swollen ER, while apoptosis is delayed, implying that mitochondrial integrity is compromised but tightly regulated; RalF and RARP-2 have been implicated in membrane-trafficking and ER–mitochondria crosstalk, with RARP-2 linked to ER remodeling that interfaces with mitochondrial apoptosis pathways, suggesting mitochondrial targeting or perturbation via organelle–organelle signaling <cite id="c5d8acbe-0">TEM shows mitochondrial damage and ER stress early in infection; cytochrome c release occurs early while apoptosis is delayed, suggesting Rickettsia modulates mitochondrial permeability; RARP-2 is proposed to alter ER structure and ER-dependent apoptotic signaling</cite>. 
- Virulence-associated mitochondrial substrates: Orthologs of mitochondrial electron transport components occur in Rickettsia (e.g., petD-like genes and cytochrome c homologs in spotted fever group), reflecting ancestral alpha-proteobacterial metabolism; their presence in pathogenic lineages suggests potential targeting or mimicry of mitochondrial respiratory machinery to siphon ATP or avoid immune detection, although direct subcellular localization data remain limited in many cases <cite id="c5d8acbe-3">Rickettsia exhibit near-mitochondrial respiratory gene complements and ATP production comparable to mitochondria, supporting a model in which virulence factors may interface with mitochondrial bioenergetics</cite>.

Plasma membrane and membrane trafficking organelles
- PI3K and PI4K effectors: Risk1 (PI3K) and RalF (Sec7-domain PI4 kinase) are delivered by the Rvh T4SS to remodel membrane phosphoinositides at the plasma membrane and trafficking organelles, promoting actin polymerization, membrane rearrangements, and formation of transient vacuoles that facilitate internalization and intracellular survival <cite id="beef7575-4">Risk1 promotes R. typhi intracellular survival by modulating PI metabolism, reflecting targeting of plasma membrane and trafficking membranes</cite> <cite id="beef7575-4">RalF is a Sec7-domain protein translocated by the Rvh system that targets phosphoinositide metabolism during invasion</cite>. 
- Actin and membrane remodeling: Early in infection, Rickettsiae trigger cytoskeletal actin polymerization and plasma membrane rearrangements to create a temporary intracellular vacuole that is rapidly lysed to avoid lysosomal destruction, indicating direct engagement of membrane remodeling effectors and host cytoskeleton <cite id="beef7575-4">Rickettsiae induce host cytoskeletal actin polymerization and plasma membrane rearrangements, forming a temporary intracellular vacuole to avoid lysosomal destruction</cite>.

- Orientia homologs in membrane trafficking: Orientia tsutsugamushi expresses OmpA/OmpD with long cytosolic tails and shares RalF/RARP-2-like effectors, paralleling Rickettsia’s membrane–organelle targeting strategy to manipulate PI metabolism and ER structures during uptake <cite id="2b287fb9-0">O. tsutsugamushi employs OmpA/OmpD homologs and T4SS effectors (RalF, RARP-2) to modulate ER structures and phosphoinositide metabolism during invasion</cite>.

Species- and pathway-specific effector repertoires
- Conservation and diversity of sca/rhff/RalF/RARP-2 across Rickettsia: Comparative genomics shows sca gene families are present in SFG and AFG rickettsiae, with species-specific expansions and deletions; virulence-associated effectors (RalF, RARP-2) are broadly conserved among pathogenic species and linked to ER/autophagy modulation, whereas nonpathogenic Rickettsia often fail to robustly hijack autophagy, consistent with differences in organelle-targeting effectors <cite id="2b287fb9-0">Phenotypic differences in autophagy evasion map to effector repertoires including Risk1, Pat1/2, and RalF/RARP-2</cite> <cite id="2b287fb9-3">sca genes (OmpA/OmpB and related autotransporters) are active in adhesion/entry and are variably conserved across species</cite> <cite id="c5d8acbe-4">Across nine Rickettsia genomes, sca genes range from two in R. prowazekii to 10 in R. felis, with sca1/4/5 conserved but variable in other lineages</cite>. 
- Host-range tailoring: Metagenome-informed analyses indicate that Rickettsia rvh effectors are distributed with lineage-specific biases and duplicated/recombined architectures, supporting that effector targeting (e.g., ER/autophagy/mitochondria) is tuned to distinct eukaryotic hosts and infection niches <cite id="c5d8acbe-2">Rickettsia rvh effectors show lineage-biased distribution and strong signatures of gene duplication and lateral transfer, implying effector architectures are tailored to discrete host cell functions</cite>.

What remains uncertain and how to resolve it
- Direct mitochondrial localization of specific effectors (e.g., Csd1-like cyt c mimics, petD homologs) is less clearly documented than ER/autophagy/PM targets; future subcellular fractionation and organelle-specific knockout/auxin-inducible degron systems for individual effectors, alongside proteomic mapping of effector-organelle association, will clarify whether these proteins localize to mitochondria or act via ER–mitochondria signaling <cite id="c5d8acbe-0">TEM reveals mitochondrial damage and ER stress early in infection, but precise mechanisms of mitochondrial permeability modulation by effectors remain to be elucidated</cite>.

Summary
- ER-targeting effectors include OmpA/OmpB-like autotransporters (RARP-2) and PI metabolism modulators (RalF, Risk1), which remodel ER structure and phosphoinositide signaling to promote uptake and cytosolic survival <cite id="c5d8acbe-0">RARP-2 alters ER structure and ER-dependent apoptotic signaling</cite> <cite id="beef7575-4">RalF and Risk1 are translocated to modulate ER and plasma membrane phosphoinositides</cite>.
